title: Stellar Parallax
body:
**Parallax** is the apparent shift of a nearby object against a distant background when the
observer moves. Holding a finger up and blinking alternate eyes demonstrates it, and the shift
shrinks as the finger moves away.

For stars the baseline is Earth's orbit, so the observations are taken six months apart and the
star's position is compared against far more distant stars.

$$
d \text{ (parsecs)} = \frac{1}{p \text{ (arcseconds)}}
$$

where $p$ is half the total annual shift.

```
Proxima Centauri:  p = 0.768"
   d = 1/0.768 = 1.30 pc = 4.25 light-years
```

This is the only direct distance measurement in astronomy and the foundation of every other
one, since the standard candles used further out are calibrated against stars whose distances
came from parallax.

Its reach is the limitation. The angles are already tiny at the nearest stars, and they shrink
with distance, so ground-based measurement fails beyond about 100 pc and space missions reach a
few thousand. Past that the [[Inverse-Square Law]] with a known luminosity takes over.
